title: Plug a fibre patch cable's SFP end into an upright network card's port, using both arms
instruction: Take the cable's gold SFP plug out of its slanted holder, stand it upright, and push it, tip first, all the way down into the network card's port nearer the robot (the card stands upright and its ports face up). The cable's blue SC plug stays in its tray. Both arms may be used.
context: Patching fibre into a server's network card (an SFP port) is routine data-centre and telecom work (O*NET 49-2011.00, 15-1231.00, 49-2022.00), and a half-seated connector causes hard-to-trace link faults. The plug fits with about 0.13 mm of play per side and starts slanted at 45 degrees with a cable dragging on it, so one arm must hold the cable while the other re-orients and inserts the plug.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases (x forward, y left), on the station table. Network card: a PCIe card model (green PCB, steel parts), standing upright on a steel foot, its face toward the left arm (its two ports side by side along x); only its upper part is modelled, 12 cm wide, 2.1 cm thick, fixed. Its top edge carries two steel SFP ports whose openings face straight up: each 14.0 mm wide, 9.0 mm tall and 48.9 mm deep inside, 23.2 mm apart, the middle between the two mouths at x 30, y 8, 7 cm above the table. Target port: the one nearer the robot (smaller x, x 28.8). Each mouth has a 2 mm flared lead-in made of four thin steel plates at 45 degrees. Cable: a yellow fibre cable, 5 mm thick, 12 g, a chain of 20 mm segments with soft bending joints, friction 1.2. Its SFP plug (gold) is a rigid body 47.3 mm long, 13.75 mm wide and 8.6 mm tall, 20 g, with a 14 x 12.2 mm latch end 11.5 mm long; it lies in a fixed steel holder (plate, two side rails 17 mm apart with lips, end stop under its tip) that leans it 45 degrees, tip down toward +y, its back end up toward -y, origin at x 24, y 30. Its SC plug (blue) is a 26 x 25 x 10 mm, 40 g body lying in a fixed steel tray at x 14, y -10 and held in place, the cable leaving its back end and draping over the table to the SFP plug. Holder, tray and card stand on thin steel base plates. One fixed starting layout.
scoring: Measured on the SFP plug's tip: depth is how far its tip is below the port mouth, along the port's axis. 1.0: tip depth at least 40 mm in the target port, plug within 3 degrees of the port axis, and the plug at rest (under 3 cm/s) at the end of a 1 s hold. 0.5: depth at least 20 mm in the target port, within 10 degrees of the port axis. 0.25: depth at least 5 mm in the target port, same angle as 0.5. Otherwise 0. The tip must also be within 1.5 mm of the port's centre line, at any depth. Any other outcome scores 0, including the other port or a plug that falls off the table. Real-world check: at 40 mm depth, at most about 7 mm of the plug body is still outside the port, and a phone level on the plug reads within 3 degrees of vertical.
reset_notes: Lay the SFP plug back in its slanted holder, tip down against the stop, and the SC plug in its tray; the cable settles in about 1.5 s.
fidelity: Plug and port sizes are the box colliders of the public AIC SFP module and NIC card models (Apache-2.0), unmodified: the port is 14.0 x 9.0 mm inside and the plug body 13.75 x 8.6 mm, so the clearance is about 0.13 mm a side in width, as in the real models. The one addition is a 2 mm flared lead-in at each port mouth, which a real cage also has, to let an open-loop robot land the plug in simulation. The plug stops at about 41.5 mm depth where its latch shoulder meets the port, so full depth is scored at 40 mm. Only the card's upper part is modelled, and it is set about 5 cm lower than a real card in a chassis so the arm can reach it with the plug upright. The cable is a 12 g soft chain of rigid segments, not a real fibre: no twisting stiffness, lighter than a real patch cable, and no latch spring, click, electrical or optical contact, so no insertion force. The plug shapes are boxes, not the detailed meshes.
